title: Shoulder dystocia
blurb: Recognise shoulder dystocia, call for help, start McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, avoid fundal pressure and non-axial traction, and document and follow up (RCOG GTG 42, 3rd edition).
question: Grace's baby's head is born on the labour ward, but routine axial traction does not deliver the shoulders. What should the midwife do first, and what must she avoid?

teach.body: Formally (RCOG GTG 42, 3rd edition): shoulder dystocia is a vaginal cephalic birth that requires additional manoeuvres to release the impacted shoulder after the head has been born and routine traction has failed. A head-to-body interval of more than 60 seconds has also been proposed as an objective definition. In plain English: the head is out but a shoulder is stuck, usually the anterior shoulder behind the mother's pubic bone (less often the posterior shoulder on the sacral promontory), and gentle routine traction will not free it.

teach.body: GTG 42 teaching starts with the quick external measures that need no special equipment: the McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure, with axial traction only. If these fail, the senior team moves on to internal manoeuvres or other measures as set out in GTG 42 and practised in local skills drills. The guideline does not describe the practical manoeuvres in detail because they need hands-on training.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Grace on the labour ward
teach.body: The head is born but routine axial traction fails. The midwife notes the time, presses the emergency bell and calls 'shoulder dystocia' for senior obstetric and neonatal help. With two helpers she brings Grace into the McRoberts position, and a colleague applies suprapubic pressure while she uses axial traction only. Nobody applies fundal pressure. A colleague records times and actions. After the birth the midwife prepares for PPH, checks the perineum and hands the baby to the neonatal team.

teach.text: Fundal pressure is the classic wrong move: it worsens the impaction. The other is pulling harder or downwards: traction stays axial. Do not learn a fixed order of internal manoeuvres from this lesson: follow GTG 42 3rd edition and your unit's skills drills.

summary: You can now recognise shoulder dystocia, call for help and start McRoberts with suprapubic pressure, while avoiding fundal pressure and non-axial traction. You can also anticipate PPH and perineal injury afterwards and document the emergency fully.

A.q: A student midwife asks how RCOG GTG 42 defines shoulder dystocia. Which answer is correct?
options: Extra manoeuvres needed after routine traction fails
A head-to-body interval of more than 10 seconds
Delay in crowning of the head for over 5 minutes
Any baby born weighing over 4.5 kg after a long labour
A.why: GTG 42: a vaginal cephalic birth that requires additional manoeuvres to release the impacted shoulder after the head is born and routine traction has failed.

whyNot.1: The proposed objective interval is more than 60 seconds, not 10.
whyNot.2: Delay in crowning concerns the head, before shoulder dystocia can occur.
whyNot.3: Birthweight does not define shoulder dystocia.

A.q: The baby's head is born and routine axial traction fails to deliver the shoulders. After calling for help, which manoeuvres come first?
options: Firm downward traction on the head
Wait for the next contraction to push
A.why: GTG 42 teaching: call for help, then the McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure as the first manoeuvres.

whyNot.0: Fundal pressure should not be used in shoulder dystocia.
whyNot.1: Downward traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury.
whyNot.3: Waiting does not release the impacted shoulder and wastes time.

A.q: Which action should be avoided during shoulder dystocia?
A.why: Fundal pressure should not be used: it can worsen the impaction of the shoulder.

whyNot.0: Calling for help is the first step.
whyNot.2: Suprapubic pressure is a first-line manoeuvre.

B.q: During shoulder dystocia, in which direction should traction on the baby's head be applied?
options: Strong traction timed with each push
Twisting traction to rotate the head
Axial, in line with the fetal spine
B.why: Traction should be axial (in line with the fetal spine); excessive or downward traction raises the risk of brachial plexus injury.

whyNot.0: Downward traction is associated with brachial plexus injury.
whyNot.1: Excessive traction is avoided whatever the timing.
whyNot.2: Twisting the head risks nerve injury and does not free the shoulder.

B.q: After a shoulder dystocia, which maternal complications is the woman at increased risk of?
B.why: GTG 42: maternal morbidity is increased, particularly PPH (11%) and obstetric anal sphincter injury (3.8%).

whyNot.0: Pre-eclampsia is not a consequence of shoulder dystocia.
whyNot.2: Cord prolapse and vasa praevia occur before the birth, not as a result of dystocia.
whyNot.3: Abruption and APH are antenatal or intrapartum events before the birth of the head.

B.q: Which fetal complication does GTG 42 describe as one of the most important after shoulder dystocia?
B.why: GTG 42: brachial plexus injury is one of the most important fetal complications, affecting 2.3-16% of births with shoulder dystocia.

whyNot.0: Jaundice is not a specific complication of shoulder dystocia.
whyNot.1: Cephalohaematoma is more associated with instrumental birth.
whyNot.3: Talipes is a congenital condition, not caused by the birth.

C.q: Help has been called, and McRoberts and suprapubic pressure have not released the shoulder. The registrar is arriving. A student offers to push on the top of the uterus. What should the midwife say?
options: Apply fundal pressure with the next push
Decline: fundal pressure is not used
Ask the woman to stand and push
C.why: Fundal pressure should not be used in shoulder dystocia. If first-line measures fail, the senior team moves to further manoeuvres per GTG 42 and local training.

whyNot.0: Fundal pressure can worsen the impaction.
whyNot.1: Stronger or downward traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury.
whyNot.3: Standing to push is not a recognised manoeuvre and loses time.

C.q: Rhiannon's baby is born after shoulder dystocia. What is the priority for Rhiannon in the next hour?
options: Anticipate PPH and check for perineal trauma
Delay the third stage for an hour of skin-to-skin
Discharge within 6 hours as low risk
Avoid examining the perineum for 24 hours
C.why: Shoulder dystocia is an intrapartum PPH risk factor (NG235 1.10.30) and raises the risk of anal sphincter injury, so she needs PPH vigilance and a systematic perineal assessment (NG235 1.12.5).

whyNot.1: Skin-to-skin is encouraged, but the third stage should not be left unmanaged when PPH risk is raised.
whyNot.2: She is at increased risk and needs observation, not early discharge.
whyNot.3: The perineum should be assessed systematically after birth, not delayed.

C.q: The midwife is writing up a shoulder dystocia. Which set of details is essential?
options: The woman's BMI and booking blood results
The baby's birthweight and the Apgar score at 10 minutes
A brief summary written the next day
Times, manoeuvres used, staff present, cord gases
C.why: Documentation should include times (head and body), the manoeuvres used and when, staff present and their arrival times, and cord blood gases (GTG 42), recorded at the time or as soon as possible (Code 10.1).

whyNot.0: Booking details are already in the notes and are not the essential record of the event.
whyNot.1: Birthweight and Apgar scores are recorded, but the times and manoeuvres are essential.
whyNot.2: Records should be completed at the time or as soon as possible, in full.

reteach.title: Hands up, not down
reteach.question: Imagine the head is out and nothing moves. What instinct must you resist, and what do you do instead?

blocks.body: The instinct is to pull harder or push on the top of the uterus. Both are wrong: harder or downward traction stretches the baby's brachial plexus, and fundal pressure jams the shoulder more firmly behind the pubic bone. Instead: call for help, change the mother's position (McRoberts), press just above the pubic bone (suprapubic pressure) and keep any traction gentle and axial while the team arrives.

blocks.text: Suprapubic pressure (just above the pubic bone) helps; fundal pressure (top of the uterus) harms. Do not confuse the two.

explain.body: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when routine axial traction fails to deliver the shoulders after the head is born. A head-to-body interval of more than 60 seconds has been proposed as an objective definition (GTG 42).

test.q: Which head-to-body interval has been proposed as an objective definition of shoulder dystocia?
test.why: GTG 42: a prolonged head-to-body delivery time of more than 60 seconds has been proposed.

whyNot.0: 10 seconds is within a normal head-to-body interval.
whyNot.2: 5 minutes is far beyond the proposed definition.
whyNot.3: 2 minutes is longer than the proposed 60-second definition.

explain.body: The first step is to call for help, stating 'shoulder dystocia' so the senior obstetric and neonatal teams know what to bring. One person records times and actions.

test.q: What is the first action when a midwife recognises shoulder dystocia?
options: Call for senior and neonatal help
Apply strong downward traction to the head
test.why: Calling for help is the first step, before and alongside McRoberts and suprapubic pressure (GTG 42).

whyNot.1: Fundal pressure should not be used.
whyNot.2: Downward traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury.
whyNot.3: Pushing harder does not release the impacted shoulder.

explain.body: McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure are the simple external first-line manoeuvres, used with axial traction only.

test.q: Which pair are the first-line manoeuvres for shoulder dystocia?
test.why: GTG 42 teaching: McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure, with axial traction only.

whyNot.1: Fundal pressure is avoided, even with McRoberts.

explain.body: GTG 42 reports PPH in 11% and obstetric anal sphincter injury in 3.8% of women, and brachial plexus injury in 2.3-16% of babies.

test.q: About what proportion of women have a PPH after shoulder dystocia, according to GTG 42?
test.why: GTG 42 reports postpartum haemorrhage in 11% of women after shoulder dystocia.

whyNot.2: 3.8% is the rate of obstetric anal sphincter injury.
